issues.legal_issue: Failure to comply with a consent order does not amount to contempt when no clear undertaking to the court was given.
material_facts: A consent order appointed a receiver to take charge of and run a business, directed the appellant not to interfere with the receiver, and required the appellant to provide cooperation the receiver might require.

The order did not expressly direct the appellant to hand over possession, and no application, affidavit, or undertaking incorporated into the order stated that the appellant had undertaken to hand over possession.
The appellant was convicted of contempt for failing to hand over possession to the receiver.
issues.conclusion: The failure to comply with the consent order did not amount to contempt in the absence of a clear undertaking to the court; the contempt conviction and sentence were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, a consent order or compromise decree is distinct from an undertaking to the court. A breach of a consent order ordinarily concerns the parties, and may be addressed through enforcement or execution under the Code of Civil Procedure, rather than contempt. The court may not infer an undertaking that is absent from the record. The principle that an undertaking must be carefully construed is supported by Bhatnagar & Co. Ltd. v. Union of India; the purposes of contempt proceedings and the need for care in exercising contempt powers are discussed in Aligarh Municipal Board v. Ekka Tanga Mazdoor Union.

predicates.contempt_appeal: A party appealed a finding that the party had committed contempt.
predicates.consent_order_not_complied_with: A party failed to comply with an order made by the court with the parties’ consent.
predicates.no_clear_undertaking: The alleged contemnor did not clearly undertake to the court, in a filed application or affidavit or in an oral statement incorporated into the court’s order, to perform the act said to have been breached.

issues.definition: When a party appeals a contempt finding based on noncompliance with a consent order, and no clear undertaking was given to the court, the breach is not contempt.

issues.legal_issue: A wilful breach of a clear undertaking given to the court may amount to contempt.
material_facts: The contempt allegation was based on an asserted undertaking to hand over possession to a receiver.
The record contained no application or affidavit giving that undertaking and the court’s order did not expressly incorporate an oral undertaking to that effect.
The court distinguished a breach of an undertaking to the court from a breach of a consent order between parties.
issues.conclusion: A wilful breach of an undertaking amounts to contempt when the undertaking was clearly and expressly given to the court, either in a filed application or affidavit or orally and incorporated into the court’s order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 applies to wilful breach of a clear undertaking given to the court. The undertaking must be carefully construed to determine its nature and extent; it cannot be assumed from the terms of an order. Bhatnagar & Co. Ltd. v. Union of India supports careful construction of the undertaking, and Aligarh Municipal Board v. Ekka Tanga Mazdoor Union explains the purposes of contempt proceedings and the need for care in exercising the power.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A court is considering whether a person’s conduct amounts to contempt.
predicates.clear_undertaking_given: A person clearly and expressly undertook to the court, in a filed application or affidavit or in an oral statement incorporated into the court’s order, to do or refrain from doing something.
predicates.undertaking_wilfully_breached: The person deliberately failed to honour the undertaking given to the court.

issues.definition: When a person clearly undertakes something to the court and deliberately fails to honour that undertaking, the wilful breach is contempt.
